title: Dropped Name
passages:
Dawn bled pale across Anza's ore stub, the kind of light that shows every crack in the rail ties and every oil stain on the concrete. The blank rig was already a shrinking coal on the northbound line, its hand lamp a wobbling orange eye retreating toward the Blank. No transponder pulse. No board entry. Just eleven warm canisters and a flame in a crew box window, rolling north on stolen momentum.

Kass walked the empty siding with their boots kicking up rail dust, the pedal-rail shed yawning dark behind them. Anza's chain had gone green again at 08:00 — Teodoro's trick with Voss's name — but the node still tasted like held breath. Clearances stripped. Resupply frozen until the re-list took. Nour's chalk still held forty names under an amber chain that hadn't been amber since morning.

A flash of white in the gray dust. Kass stopped, boot heel grinding it flat.

A coast ticket. Heavy card stock, folded sharp into thirds the way you fold something you mean to keep. The bought name on the face meant nothing — *J. RENNER, TRANSIT CLASS, VALID THROUGH WINTER* — but the graphite thumbprint smudged into the corner, and the deep crease from a coat pocket's hard edge: those were Miko's. Kass had watched Miko fold tickets that way a dozen times. Pocket, unfold, check, pocket. The rhythm of someone who didn't trust anything to stay put.

Kass picked it up with two fingers, turned it over. Blank back. No stamp. No punch. If the ticket was here, its owner wasn't. And Miko had three of these things under three different names, paid for with cargo weight Kass didn't want to know about.

The wind shifted, carrying the rig's diesel ghost south. The hand lamp bobbed once, steady as a breath held.

Kass slipped the ticket into their own pocket, coat crease matching coat crease, and kept walking the siding toward the pedal-rail shed. The ore line stretched north, empty and patient. Culvert Nine sat penciled on Anza's board in Saul's careful hand — proposed, not live. A dead pump station with a live storeroom and a woman who'd marked it in her own name.

Kass's badge caught the light, thin and bent at one corner. They had a tally card cleared, a glove with a cut palm, and a chip match made but not read out. They had a thread they wouldn't drop.

The pedal-rail waited in its shed, chain dry, bearing ready to shriek. Past the first node, there was no one left to call.

The relay shop's side door stuck on its track, metal grinding metal. Kass shouldered it open and stepped into the cool dark, letting the door swing shut behind them. Dawn light sliced through the high windows, catching dust motes and the green chain marker snapped into its slot on the resupply board.

*CHAIN RESTORED — VOSS RE-LISTED 08:00 — RESUPPLY LIVE*

Teodoro's handwriting, cramped and precise. The board was black-painted steel, chalk lines ruled in white. Shift roster at the top, resupply notes below. Kass read down the names with the ticket burning in their coat pocket.

Nour — Shift 1 Lead. Doan — *CLEARANCE WITHDRAWN* scratched red beside it. Teodoro — Reader Two. Wren Cardoso — *SHOP HAND — COUNTERSIGNED 2244*, fresh chalk still dusting the letters.

Fifth line down: *MIKO — RESUPPLY LOADER*.

The checkmark box beside it was scraped clean. Not erased — *scraped*, like someone had taken a knife to it. The chalk outline of the mark remained, ghost-white against black steel. The shift had formed. The shift had left. Miko's name stayed on the board, but her body hadn't shown up for the roll call.

Kass's thumb found the ticket's folded edge through the wool. *J. Renner*. One of three names Miko had bought. Three tickets, three chances at the coast. She'd used none of them to leave.

Below the roster, in a different hand — pencil, careful print, pressed hard enough to groove the steel:

*PROPOSED RESUPPLY: CULVERT NINE*

No time stamp. No reader initials. No green chain marker beside it. Just Saul's handwriting and a dead station name. Culvert Nine. A pump station that hadn't pumped in fifteen years, its storeroom sealed and its jaw rusted shut — until Odessa Brill had marked it in her own name and the receiving jaw had started reading cargo again.

Eleven warm canisters on a blank rig. Nour's eleven short seals, struck full at Anza's jaw, paid out to Brill's storeroom to keep Anza eating through winter. The rig had pulled out at 06:47 by Teodoro's log. Two hours fourteen minutes ago. The ore line grade was steady but long — two and a half hours to Culvert Nine's switch if the rig held speed, three if it didn't.

The hand lamp had been burning in the crew box window. Steady. Fed. Someone was on that rig, watching the flame.

Kass stood between the scraped slot and the penciled name. The ticket in their pocket. The glove with its cut palm at their hip. The tally card cleared in their bag.

The rig was hours ahead. The canisters were headed for a jaw that faulted on skims. And Miko was on that rig — or she wasn't, and the ticket in Kass's pocket was the only proof she'd ever been there at all.

The shop door banged open behind them.

Doan filled the doorway, then the room, shoulders hunched like the cold had followed them in. Their wrists were bare — the orange locker cord cut and coiled at their belt, the frayed end swinging every time they moved. No key on the loop. Nothing left to open.

Kass turned from the board. "You're meant to be at the stub."

"I was." Doan let the door bang shut behind them. "Got no clearance, no key that works, and a wrist that itches where Wren's knife went through the cord. She logged it like I'm freight." They rubbed the bare wrist. "So I walked up. Figured somebody ought to say the thing nobody said at six forty-seven."

Kass kept one hand in their pocket, thumb on the ticket's fold. "Say it, then."

Doan crossed to the board, read the scraped fifth line, and their mouth went flat. "You already know half. You've got that look — the one where you've decided something stupid and you're just waiting on a reason to." They tipped their chin at the window, at the north line beyond it. "Rig pulled out while I was standing there with a dead key in my hand, feeling sorry for myself. I watched it go."

"Everyone watched it go."

"Not the way I did." Doan leaned on the ledge, next to Nour's chalk. "There was a woman in a coast coat. One of the good ones, the waxed kind you save for the coast train, not for standing around an ore stub at dawn. She didn't walk to it. She ran, caught the grab rail when it was already rolling, and swung herself up into the crew box."

Kass went still. The crew box — the little steel compartment on the nose of a rig where a person rides when the machine needs eyes, cramped and cold, meant for a spotter, not a passenger.

"Then she leaned out," Doan went on, "and hung a hand lamp in the window. Lit. Set it in the frame so it'd hold. And the rig took the north switch and the coal just kept bobbing off like it had somewhere to be."

"Did you call out?"

Doan laughed, short and ugly. "To who? No transponder, no board, no driver. And she had a coat for the coast and she was climbing the wrong way on purpose." They spread their hands. "Nobody asks, out here. You learn that or you learn it the hard way, and I already learned it the hard way this morning." The frayed cord swung. "So no. I didn't ask. I watched somebody ride north with your canisters and figured, well — now there's two who'll freeze instead of one."

The hand lamp. Kass thought of it burning in that little window. Not a signal. Not a flare. Just a flame somebody had bothered to set and keep. You didn't hang a lamp for a rig; the rig didn't need to see. You hung it for whoever came looking.

"Two tickets," Kass said, before they could stop it. Then, at the narrowing in Doan's eyes: "Nothing. Forget I said it."

Doan didn't forget it. Doan never forgot anything — that was the whole trouble with them; they saw everything and asked for none of it. But they only pushed off the ledge and jerked their chin at the door. "Pedal-rail's in the shed. Chain's dry. Bearing's screaming already — I heard it coming past. Two and a half hours to the Culvert switch if you keep the pedals turning." A beat. "She's got two hours on you and a warm box."

Kass was already moving. "Then I'd best not stand here talking to a man with no key."

"Load's not a man either," Doan said to their back, "and here we both are, come the bell."

Kass didn't look back. The shed door was twenty feet of frozen gravel and they ate it in four strides, badge already in hand, the ticket's folded corner pressing a hard line against their ribs through the wool.

The pedal-rail sat in the dark like a dead thing — steel frame, two narrow wheels fore and aft, a crossbar seat bolted to the chassis, and two sets of pedals chained to the drive axle. No motor. No battery. No radio. Just leverage and leg and a man or woman willing to burn themselves down to nothing for the distance. The ore line's only backup when the rigs wouldn't run and the nodes couldn't wait.

Kass dropped to one knee, fingers finding the chain. Dry as bone. The links didn't flex; they *cracked*. The rear bearing was a rusted puck seated in a housing that had seen grease maybe once this decade. They dug the oil can from the shelf — Teodoro's private stash, thick and black and labeled *FOR CHAIN ONLY* in fading marker — and worked it into every joint, wrist turning until the metal drank it down. The bearing shrieked a test rotation, high and thin, like a bird with a broken wing.

"Sign it out," Teodoro's voice from the shelf, or maybe just the rule speaking through habit. *No pedal-rail leaves the shed without a badge number and a return time chalked on the frame.*

Kass stood, wiped their hands on their thighs, and pulled the chalk from the ledge. Their badge number: *K-774*. Return: *BEFORE SHIFT BELL — 18:00*. They wrote it large on the crossbar, dust puffing white.

The shed log was a clipboard bolted to the wall, pages yellowed at the edges. Kass flipped to a clean line, wrote the date, the badge, the rig ID stamped on the frame — *PR-ANZA-03* — and the destination line. They hesitated, chalk hovering.

*CULVERT NINE — PROPOSED*

Not live. Not authorized. Just proposed. But the rig was already north with Anza's food, and Miko was on it, and the jaw at Culvert Nine would fault on skims if nobody met it with the right key. Kass pressed the chalk down hard. *PROPOSED* became *LIVE* with one stroke.

They clipped the clipboard shut, swung a leg over the crossbar, and settled onto the seat. The pedals were cold alloy, the chains taut. First push would tell the truth of the bearing.

Kass looked south once, toward the relay shop's side door. Doan's silhouette stood in the frame, a dark cutout against the green chain light. No wave. No call. Just two people who knew the math: the rig had two hours and a warm box. The pedal-rail had legs that would scream before the first node, and past that node there was no one left to call.

First push. The chain bit. The bearing groaned, then settled into a rhythm — *clack-hiss, clack-hiss* — and the pedal-rail rolled out of the shed onto the ore line's northbound rail, eating distance one burning stroke at a time.

Anza's ore stub fell behind. The Blank opened ahead, flat and pale, the hand lamp a wobbling coal two hours north and pulling away.
